title: Hassett is saying there's going to be a reconcilia...
content:
Hassett is saying there's going to be a reconciliation bill next year and that Congress has more fiscal room to do stimulus than people realize. 
He's basically claiming the administration's tariff revenue and deficit math is working better than expected, which opens up space in that reconciliation bill to fund things like Trump's $2,000 stimulus checks or whatever other priorities they want to push through.​
Reconciliation is Congress's special process for passing major tax and spending bills without needing 60 Senate votes, it only needs a simple majority. 
When they use reconciliation, they get a budget score that says you can increase the deficit by X amount over ten years.
If your proposals come in under that number, you've got extra room to add more stuff.
Hassett's saying the fiscal position is better than people thought, so they've got more room in that budget than originally expected. 
Basically, if tariffs are bringing in more revenue and the deficit is improving faster than anticipated, that means they can fit more spending and tax cuts into next year's reconciliation package without blowing past their limit.​
This is a signal about what's coming in 2026, and it's worth noting that Hassett is also the leading candidate to be the next Federal Reserve chairman. 
The administration is signaling they won't be fiscally constrained when building that reconciliation bill, so expect bigger stimulus and spending proposals. 
They will keep this economy running hot at least till the midterms.

title: Over 31% of all U.S. wealth is now held by people ...
content:
Over 31% of all U.S. wealth is now held by people over 70 years old and this share has been steadily climbing since the mid 1990s. 
Think of it like this, back in the 90s, people over 70 controlled roughly 20% of the nation's wealth, but that number has grown almost 60% over the past three decades.
 he gray bars on the chart mark major economic disruptions like recessions, and what's interesting is that every time the economy took a hit, older Americans actually became richer relative to the rest of the population.
The 2008 financial crisis, the dot com crash, and the pandemic all show this same pattern where their share of wealth jumped or stayed resilient while everyone else got hammered.
Younger and middle aged Americans are essentially getting priced out of wealth accumulation. 
When a 70 year old owns a house worth $500k that they paid $50k for in 1980, and a 35 year old is trying to buy that same house for $500k with student loans and stagnant wages, the wealth gap compounds every single year. 
This isn't just about investment returns either. It's about who owns real estate, who has paid off their mortgages, and who locked in assets decades ago before prices exploded. 
Meanwhile, younger generations are starting from further back, dealing with higher asset prices, and having less time to compound their wealth before they retire.
The implications are actually pretty significant for society and the market. 
First, you've got potential policy risk because this creates intergenerational tension. When millennials and Gen Z realize they're essentially locked out of the wealth that older generations accumulated, you'll see pressure for taxes on capital gains, inheritance taxes, and maybe even wealth taxes. 
Second, it affects consumer spending and economic growth because younger people with less wealth spend differently than older people just managing their portfolios. 
Third, from a market perspective, expect shifting sector preferences as Baby Boomers gradually liquidate assets and healthcare, consumer staples, and dividend plays might outperform growth stocks. 
The wealth transfer that's about to happen over the next 10-20 years will be huge but not everyone's inheriting anything, so the wealth gap might actually get worse before it gets better.
More than 31% of all wealth is held by people over 70 years old.
(h/t Torsten Slok) https://t.co/Uu51p9ejBK 
-

title: Fed has finished a big multi year cleanup of its b...
content:
Fed has finished a big multi year cleanup of its balance sheet after the huge money printing during Covid but it stopped shrinking things while the balance sheet is still very large by historical standards. 
The balance sheet is now around 6.5 trillion dollars, which is down a lot from the peak, but still far above the roughly 4 trillion area before the pandemic. 
The Fed did this by letting the bonds it owns mature without fully replacing them, which slowly pulled money out of the financial system and reversed a bit more than half of the emergency support it added in 2020–2021.
In beginner terms, you can think of the Fed’s balance sheet as a big pool of money and bonds that helps determine how much cash is sloshing around in banks and markets. 
During quantitative easing (QE), the Fed filled the pool by buying bonds, which pushed cash into the system and tended to support asset prices. 
Quantitative tightening (QT) was the opposite: the Fed let that pool drain, which removed cash and made financial conditions tighter. 
Now that QT has ended, the Fed is basically saying this is as small as we’re comfortable going for now because they don’t want to risk another plumbing problem like the 2019 repo spike where markets suddenly ran short of safe cash and short term rates jumped.
The implications going forward are that one important source of tightening pressure is gone, but policy is still restrictive through interest rates. 
Markets no longer have to worry about the Fed being a constant, predictable seller of Treasuries and mortgage bonds, which is mildly supportive for stocks, credit, and longer term bonds because there is less forced supply hitting the market every month. 
At the same time, the Fed has kept the balance sheet big enough that banks still have a comfortable cushion of reserves, so it has more room to focus on deciding when to cut rates based on inflation and growth rather than on avoiding a liquidity accident.
 If the economy and inflation keep cooling, this setup (no more QT plus eventual rate cuts) leans supportive for risk assets, if inflation flares up again, the Fed can keep rates high for longer, but is less likely to quickly restart aggressive QT given how sensitive the system is to liquidity.
BREAKING: The Federal Reserve’s balance sheet fell -$37 billion in November, to $6.53 trillion, to its lowest level since April 2020.
The Fed has reduced its assets by -$2.43 trillion, or -27%, during its quantitative tightening (QT) program, which ended on December 1st after running for 3 years and 5 months.
This unwound 51% of the +$4.81 trillion added during pandemic-era QE.
Treasury securities declined -$4 billion in November, to $4.19 trillion, the lowest since June 2020. 
We have now see a -$1.58 trillion decline in treasury securities, or -27.4%, from the June 2022 peak.
Mortgage-backed securities fell -$16 billion last month, to $2.05 trillion, the lowest since November 2020, down -$687 billion from the 2022 peak.
QT is officially over. 
- 
The Kobeissi Letter

title: People massively underestimate how many others sha...
content:
People massively underestimate how many others share their belief in the existence of intelligent extraterrestrial life, representing an outstanding case of "pluralistic ignorance".
          [Recent research] established that 58.20% of astrobiology experts believe intelligent extraterrestrial life likely exists, providing the first empirical baseline for public comparison. We surveyed 6,114 highly educated and scientifically engaged individuals to assess their beliefs about extraterrestrial intelligent life existence.
         Our investigation reveals belief dynamics that fundamentally challenge conventional science communication paradigms. The phenomenon we term the "cosmic closet" represents one of the largest documented cases of pluralistic ignorance in science communication literature. While 95.01% of participants privately believe extraterrestrial intelligence exists, they estimate only 48.94% of their social circles share this view.
         The phenomenon of pluralistic ignorance describes situations where individuals systematically misperceive peer beliefs, believing their private beliefs differ from those of their peers. [Like in the story of "The Emperor's New Clothes", where everyone could see that the Emperor was naked, but falsely assumed that everyone else genuinely saw and admired the non-existent clothing. Thus, in the end, everyone was faking it.]
         This misperception creates a self-perpetuating cycle: individuals remain silent about their beliefs, interpreting others' silence as skepticism, which reinforces their own reticence. Beliefs about extraterrestrial intelligence existence remain socially constrained despite near-universal private acceptance.
         This silence likely stems from multiple psychological and social factors. Concerns about appearing unscientific, particularly among educated populations, may suppress expression. The historical association of extraterrestrial intelligence beliefs with fringe communities and conspiracy theories creates reputational risk. Additionally, the absence of established social scripts for discussing cosmic questions leaves individuals uncertain about appropriate discourse norms.

title: The chart shows data from Revelio Labs, which trac...
content:
The chart shows data from Revelio Labs, which tracks job market activity by scraping career sites like LinkedIn and Indeed. 
They are reporting that the U.S. economy didn't just slow down in November 2025, it actually shrank. 
According to their data, we lost 9,000 jobs last month, marking the second month in a row of negative growth. 
To make matters worse, they went back and revised the data for the last four months, essentially admitting they previously overcounted by nearly 160,000 jobs. 
The trend is clear, the job market is actively deteriorating, not growing.
The scariest part of this report is who is losing jobs. 
The private sector (actual businesses that drive the economy) shed nearly 19,400 positions. 
The only reason the headline number wasn't worse is that the government added about 10,400 jobs. 
This is a classic masking effect where taxpayer funded hiring covers up the fact that corporate America has stopped hiring or started firing. 
This is a leading indicator and official government reports often lag behind real time data like this.
This is a massive red flag because if companies are posting fewer jobs and actively removing listings, it means income is about to dry up for a massive chunk of the workforce. 
When the job ladder gets pulled up like this, it doesn't hit everyone equally. It aggressively deepens the "K-shaped" economy where the people at the top with secure assets stay fine, but the average worker relying on wages sees their opportunities vanish. 
We are watching the gap between the haves and the have-nots get forced even wider in real-time.
Weakness in the US labor market is intensifying:
US nonfarm employment fell -9,000 in November, marking the 2nd consecutive monthly decline, according to Revelio.
The firm compiles data from company career pages, such as LinkedIn and Indeed, and staffing agencies.
This comes as private employment dropped -19,400 while the government added +10,400 jobs.
Furthermore, October’s decline was revised sharply lower, by -6,400 jobs, to -15,500.
This brings  total downward revisions to -158,800 over the last 4 months.
Nonfarm payrolls have now posted 5 declines over the last 7 months, the worst streak in at least 5 years.
Deterioration of the job market is accelerating.
